item.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
item.description: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

item.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
item.description: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

item.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
item.description: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

item.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
item.description: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

item.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
item.description: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. item.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
item.description: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains,

item.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
item.description: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. item.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gai

item.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
item.description: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

item.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
item.description: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.

item.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
item.description: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.

item.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
item.description: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

item.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
item.description: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, alt

item.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
item.description: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

item.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
item.description: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves

item.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
item.description: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

item.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting i

item.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
item.description: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

item.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
item.description: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

item.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
item.description: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

item.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
item.description: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.

item.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
item.description: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

item.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
item.description: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

item.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
item.description: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

item.title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
item.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.

item.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
item.description: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way

item.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
item.description: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

item.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
item.description: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

item.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
item.description: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

item.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
item.description: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining

item.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
item.description: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

item.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
item.description: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

item.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
item.description: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brai

item.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
item.description: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

item.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

item.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
item.description: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. item.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

item.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
item.description: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. item.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
item.description: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a power

item.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
item.description: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. item.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
item.description: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food

item.title: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
item.description: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

item.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

item.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
item.description: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regul

item.title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.

item.title: A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered a potentially enormous new dwarf planet beyond Pluto, hidden for years in one of the most crowded regions of the night sky. The discovery of 2026 ED138 could expand the solar system's official dwarf planet family and hints that more mysterious worlds may be lurking far beyond Neptune.

item.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
item.description: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. item.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
item.description: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
item.description: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. item.title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
item.description: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

item.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
item.description: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

item.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
item.description: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. item.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
item.description: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

item.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
item.description: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
item.description: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

item.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
item.description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a pow

item.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
item.description: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

item.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
item.description: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than som

item.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
item.description: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

item.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
item.description: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.
